reason: The typed call dispatcher, the Typert descriptors, the multiplexed stream socket and the client face are not built, because the Go host renders HTML and its handlers call services directly. What the gateway guaranteed is restated as rules: only declared routes are callable, input is decoded strictly before a handler runs, access is checked on every route, cancellation reaches the work, and live data flows on one event stream with three recovery classes.

The build-time assembly of remote namespaces and the allowlist of forwarded host events are replaced by run-time registration: a route or a stream source is an effect of the component that owns the feature, and no host event is forwarded to a browser.

The model is kept: principals, resources, roles, bindings, one policy per non-owner kind, one decision point that fails closed. Changed: every route and stream source must declare its rule or it cannot register, decisions take no request arguments, and the client-side snapshot and hooks are replaced by rendering with the same Allows function that enforces.

The Remote namespace, the follow stream and the whole client half (session manager, journal stream, submission echoes, retain references) are replaced by session routes, the stream's journal class and a small host component, conversation, that keeps the ordering rules: blank reuse under the lease, a prompt admitted once per request id, fork and manual continuation.

The two Remote streams and the reference-counted client job service become three routes and two stream interests (roster, output tail) over area A13's job registry; the human kill keeps its reason and its access is the session in the URL.

The settings and credentials Remote namespaces become owner-only form routes over area A07's settings forms and area A17's credential store. The rule that no call returns a secret value is kept and tested by scanning every response. Opening the settings file in a native editor is dropped with the desktop application; the page shows the path.

The person's terminals are kept as the userterm service: session-owned, unconfined, capped, reattached from a screen snapshot and reclaimed after confirmed idleness. Changed: the terminal session, emulator and agent terminals are area A09's service, the duplex Remote stream becomes one WebSocket per terminal, and nothing is kept in browser storage.

Create, rename, remove, reorder, archive, pin, the first-use workspace and directory picking are kept as routes over area A07's workspace registry. The follow stream becomes the shell state region of the event stream, and the client workspace model is not built.

The bounded file service is kept as wsfiles over the filesystem seam: text pages, byte reads, listing, search and watching, with reads following the backend's authority. Changed: bytes are plain HTTP with Range, the change feed becomes stream interests, and the client resource provider is replaced by host rendering.

The deprecated page entry point is kept upstream for existing web callers. The Go design has one history route, session.history, and UI routes carry no compatibility promise, so no second entry point exists to deprecate.

An unclassified failure is answered as one Problem with the code web/internal and a request id that names the log entry holding the full error chain; classified errors keep their own code from the one error table. In-process callers are ordinary Go calls and keep the wrapped error.

There is no generic uplink to give credits to. Everything a browser sends is an ordinary request with a body limit, except the terminal socket, whose protocol bounds unacknowledged bytes in both directions by acknowledgements (area A09's Attach, framed here).

SRC mode is a weaker validation path for running the host from TypeScript source, where the compiler plugin does not run. Go has no source-versus-built difference: a form is decoded strictly into a Go struct in every build.

The need for a generated codec per client-supplied field comes from TypeScript types being erased at run time and from host and client being separate builds. Go types exist at run time and there is no client contribution to mount.

Upstream leaves resume to each domain. The Go hub owns it: a stream source declares one of three recovery classes (journal resumed by cursor, state restarted from a baseline, notice that may be lost), so a feature cannot forget to define what happens after a reconnect.

Activation is a field of every route declaration (None, LiveOnly, MayResume), not a property of the lookup key, so two routes that address the same session can differ and a test lists which routes may wake a session.

No host event payload is forwarded to a browser. A change becomes a fragment rendered for the principal that reads it, so there is nothing unprojected to redact; what must survive a reconnect is a state baseline, and the notice class is declared lossy.

The event stream has a heartbeat interval and a separate write deadline, and the terminal socket a ping interval and a separate dead-after deadline, so a deployment that stalls longer than the cadence raises the deadline alone.

The per-frame compression decision works around the ws library ignoring its threshold option. There is no multiplexed socket, the event stream is never compressed and the terminal socket is uncompressed by default, so the workaround has no subject.

The compression half does not arise, and the terminal socket has end-to-end ping and pong. The event stream is one-way: behind a reverse proxy that buffers, a write succeeds into the proxy, so a vanished tab is noticed only when the proxy closes or when the stream is rotated at MaxAge.
justification: Server-sent events carry no reply from the browser, and adding one would need script and a second request path. The cost is bounded: one goroutine and one stream slot per ghost, at most MaxAge (30 minutes by default), and the per-peer cap parks the oldest stream first.

reason: The output a person sees is still a live preview: the standard output and standard error of a process are two pipes with no common clock, so their interleaving inside one read round cannot be recovered. Removed: the view no longer joins chunks blindly, each chunk is rendered with its channel.
justification: Exact interleaving needs the producer to write both streams to one pipe, which is a choice of the command, not of the job roster. The page labels chunks by channel and states that order across channels is approximate. Area A13 owns the ring.

reason: A job is a child process owned by a fiber of the host, so a host restart ends it and its output ring. The roster is a state region: after a restart its baseline is empty and replaces the stale rows, and a request for an old job answers not-found with a plain message.
justification: The design owns every child process through a fiber and stops it with the host (design.md section 4.4); a job that outlived its host would be a process nobody owns. What survives is what area A13 writes to the session log.

reason: The job routes carry the session in the URL path and declare it as their resource, so access is decided before the registry is read, and the job id must belong to the set that session can see.

A decision reads the principal, the action, the resource and the time, never request arguments, and the host renders a control by calling the same Allows function that guards its route. A page can therefore not show as allowed what the check refuses.

A route cannot register unless every path parameter is bound to a resource kind or declared opaque, a form field typed as a resource id must carry an access tag, and a handler can obtain a session or workspace id only through an accessor for a declared parameter.
Resources are never found by matching field names. They come from the URL pattern's bound parameters and from Go field types, so adding a field with a familiar name adds no resource and removes none.

There is one kind of route. Downloads, uploads, streams and the terminal socket use the same declaration with an access rule as pages and form actions, so no route sits outside the check and none needs a blanket refusal.
Answering an approval or question stays owner-only by default. The answer route declares an action on the session, so a policy could grant it without a code change, but no shipped policy does.
justification: An approval widens what the model may do, and design.md section 6 lets only an owner principal create a session grant. Whether any non-owner role may ever answer is a security decision of area A17, which owns the interaction registry.

reason: No event payload reaches a browser. A session row is rendered for the principal that sees it, through the list filter, and a link to a parent session is rendered only when that principal may see the parent.

There is no ready frame and no host-facts value: the stream sends rendered fragments only, and the harness home is not part of any of them. Residual and stated: the content of a shared session still contains the owner's absolute paths.

A grant or revocation calls Invalidate, which raises access.Changed. The hub then re-checks every open stream of that principal: a stream on a session that is no longer allowed ends, and state baselines are re-sent without the revoked rows.

The capability set is fixed by value imports because the client is a separate TypeScript build that must import generated artifacts. The Go UI has no client build: a route exists when its component is loaded.
The explicit /remote import and mount per capability is a consequence of the generated client projection and the split TypeScript faces. A Go component registers its own routes at run time.

What needs reliable recovery is no longer left to each owner: a stream source must declare its class, state sources send a complete baseline on every connection including all pending interactions, and the notice class is reserved for messages whose loss is harmless.

The work slice exists because Node runs all host work on one thread and must yield by hand. A Go list request runs on its own goroutine, is preempted by the scheduler, is cancelled through its request context, and reads one keyset page of stored rows.

The upload route stores through area A07's attachment store, whose image admission checks decoded dimensions and pixel count within fixed limits before anything is kept (areas/storage.md, untrusted image admission); the byte cap is only the first check.

A stream that fails is retried by the stream script with a bounded, growing delay for as long as the tab is open, and the page shows a host-not-reachable state meanwhile; on return the host resumes from the cursor or sends reset.
An upload is one streamed multipart request under the attachment limit; a retry sends the file again from the first byte.
justification: Resumable offsets need a second protocol and partial state on the host that must be cleaned up. On loopback an upload is a local copy; only a remote link pays for a retry. The request id still prevents a duplicate attachment.

reason: The host assigns a fork's title inside the fork command, after normalising it and against the titles the store holds, and forks of one source run one at a time, so two concurrent forks cannot pick the same increment.

The completion route is declared with Activation None: it reads the session's recorded directory and searches through the filesystem seam without creating an agent, for file references as well as for skills.

There is no display memory in the browser. Prompt acceptance is a committed inbox event, the list summary marks the session as not blank at that event, and a reloaded page is rendered from the same durable facts.

Every tab renders the session list from host state and receives the same shell replacement on the stream, so two tabs cannot disagree about whether a session is blank for longer than one event delivery.

The bound of 64 references exists for a batched describe call from the browser. The settings page is rendered by the host, which reads credential presence directly, so there is no batch call and no bound to configure.

A terminal still does not survive the host or its session's deletion, and no shell is started again automatically. Removed: exited terminals no longer count against MaxTerminals; a separate small number of exited screens is kept and the oldest is dropped.
justification: A terminal is a child process owned by a fiber (design.md section 4.4). Restoring it after a restart would mean a process that outlives its owner, or replaying a shell, which cannot restore its state. The roster region says that the previous host's terminals ended.

reason: Whether a pseudo-terminal can be allocated is still known only by opening one. Creation fails with a typed error and leaves nothing behind, because a terminal is published only after its backend is set up.
justification: Allocation depends on the operating system's state at that moment (device limits, the Windows console host), so no earlier probe proves it. Area A09 owns the provider; this area reports its error on the form.

reason: Reclamation still needs a positive idle observation, and unknown activity never counts as idle, so a terminal whose activity cannot be observed is kept until it is closed. Narrowed: area A09 reports idle or busy from the terminal's foreground process group, which does not depend on which shell runs.
justification: Treating unknown as idle would kill a person's running work. Where the operating system cannot report the foreground group, keeping the terminal is the safe failure; no maximum run time is imposed for the same reason.

reason: A new attachment gets the bounded screen and scrollback, not a transcript, and one attachment at a time writes and resizes.
justification: The bound is the memory limit per terminal, and a pseudo-terminal has one size, so two windows cannot both set it. Both are deliberate and configurable through area A09's screen settings.

reason: The workspace list is a state region: after a reconnect it is sent whole again and no increments are replayed.
justification: This is the rule for every small piece of state (DH-ADR-WIRE-3): a baseline of a few kilobytes is cheaper and simpler than a durable change log for machine state, and a whole value cannot be applied out of order.

reason: Deletion markers protect a client model from delayed data. There is no client model: each connection receives whole regions rendered from the registry in one order, so a removed workspace cannot be revived by a late frame.

When the filesystem provider of the session's world cannot watch, wsfiles polls Stat for each watched interest at PollInterval. The number of interests per tab is capped, so the polling cost is bounded, and an SSH world gets automatic refresh.
When a watch ends or fails for good, the hub replaces the region with a marker that says it is no longer live, and the polling fallback is tried first, so a view never keeps old metadata silently.

Local watching goes through the harness watch service, whose requirement covers a parent directory that is deleted and recreated; this is the same resolution the filesystem area records for the provider.
Listing, search and directory watching stay inside the session's workspace, while a named file is read wherever the filesystem backend allows.
justification: This is the read-authority decision, kept on purpose: a listing or a watch explores, a named read does not, and one read policy owned by the filesystem seam avoids a second, different check in the UI layer.

reason: A text page reports the total number of lines when the file is within the whole-file cap, counted in one pass and remembered per file version; above the cap it says that the total is unknown.
A line longer than the page byte cap is cut at a UTF-8 boundary into continuation segments, so every window makes progress and a file with one very long line can be read to its end.

Metadata is taken from the opened file, and the version is compared again after the read; a difference is reported as changed-during-read with the newer version, so a mismatch is stated instead of silent.

An invalidation is a state slot per region in the hub: a newer one replaces a waiting one, and the number of regions per tab is capped, so a tab that reads nothing holds a bounded amount of memory and is closed at the write deadline.

The entry cap still bounds the answer and not the directory read, because the filesystem seam's ReadDir returns the whole listing. Removed: the larger cost, one stat per child, since Go's directory read returns each entry's type without it.
justification: A bounded listing needs a limit or an iterator on area A08's ReadDir, which this area does not own; the request is recorded in the specification's open questions.

reason: Search uses area A08's search helper, which walks the provider of the session's world in Go and needs no packaged binary, so it works on an SSH world. A search that stops at the file cap still reports that it is incomplete.

No Go event carries list activity to a browser. The hub's shell source re-renders the affected row and its order when area A06 announces a change of the list summary, and sends it as a state replacement.

The shell source re-renders the session row for each reader when an agent is created or a workspace membership changes; the row is rendered through the access filter, so no summary payload is forwarded.
A failure outside a durable turn position becomes a notice event on the stream, raised from area A02's agent.Failed; it is declared lossy, and a failure that matters is in the session log.
The shell source replaces the affected region when an agent is disposed or a session is removed; a tab that connects later gets the current list as its baseline.
The running mark of a session row is a state region replaced when area A02 raises agent.StatusChanged; the status is in every baseline, so a missed change cannot leave it wrong.

Replaced by the Go structs stream.Config (Heartbeat, WriteTimeout, MaxAge, ReplayLimit, PageEvents, StreamsPerPeer, InterestsPerTab, TabGrace) and web.Config (MaxFormBytes, HandlerTimeout). The socket heartbeat, inbox, outbox and compression fields have no counterpart because the multiplexed socket is gone.
Replaced by routes/jobs.Config with OutputFlush (100 ms) and MaxFrameBytes (65,536), the same two values under Go names.

Replaced by conversation.Config: the history window minima and cap that upstream fixes in code. nativeOpen is dropped with the desktop application and listWorkSliceMs with the single thread it served.
Upstream's schema has no fields. The settings routes need no configuration of their own; they are present when their component is mounted.

Replaced by userterm.Config with upstream's defaults for shell choice, caps, input and buffer limits, the unattended timeout, the activity poll and the cleanup retry, plus ExitedKept. Scrollback, the stop grace and the agent terminal cap move to area A09.
Replaced by routes/workspaces.Config with DocumentsDirectory and DocumentsLookupTimeout (10 s), used by the first-use workspace route.

Replaced by wsfiles.Config with upstream's caps for pages, byte reads, lines, entries and search, plus PollInterval for the watch fallback. The process grace and stderr cap of the packaged search binary have no counterpart.
No service key replaces it. Its three operations are routes of the settings route component, which calls area A17's credential store and renders presence and a masked preview only.
No service key replaces it. Directory picking is the route directory.browse of the workspace route component, a server-rendered picker over the host filesystem, owner only.
No service key replaces it. The job routes and their two stream interests call area A13's job registry directly.
Replaced by the service key access.Key with the interface access.Service: RegisterKind, RegisterPolicy, Decide, Allows and Invalidate.
Replaced by conversation.Key with the interface Commands (Create, Prompt, Continue, Fork), which holds the ordering rules a carrier needs; reads go to area A06's query service and to the stream.
No service key replaces it. File-reference completion is the route session.complete, which searches through the filesystem seam of the session's world without waking the session.
No service key replaces it. Skill completion is the same route session.complete, reading area A14's skill catalog without waking the session.
No service key replaces it. The settings routes call area A07's settings.Forms (Describe, Apply) and render the forms; a stale write is a 409.
Replaced by userterm.Key with the interface userterm.Service for the person's terminals (create, list, rename, close, hold, reclaim); agent terminals are area A09's terminal.Key.
There is no typed call dispatcher: a handler is a Go function registered as a route and calls services directly. web.Key registers routes and dispatches no remote calls.
No service key replaces it. The workspace routes call area A07's workspace.Registry, which already serialises mutations, and the shell stream source renders its changes.
Replaced by wsfiles.Key with the interface wsfiles.Service: Stat, Text, Open, List, Search and Watch, each taking a session and bounded by wsfiles.Config.

Final verdict after reading the note: drop the mechanism, keep its purpose. Decorators, the generated client projection and the two-faced gateway exist because host and browser are separate TypeScript programs. The purpose, an explicit allowlist of what a browser may call with validated input, is kept by the route registry: only a declared route exists and its form is decoded strictly.

Final verdict: keep the three recovery rules (journal by cursor, state as whole snapshots, notifications that may be lost) and the split that the transport owner knows nothing about a feature's content. The carrier changes to server-sent events carrying fragments, and resume moves from a client journal to the host, which reads from the store by sequence number.

Final verdict: keep. A dedicated service keyed by session, with bounded line pages, byte reads and a change feed, and no file code in the session controller, is what the Go UI needs too. The client provider half and the dual-face packaging are not carried.

Final verdict: keep. Named reads follow the session filesystem backend's read authority and listing and watching stay inside the workspace. The stated exposure is restated: a file view can show any file the user can read. The preview of an HTML file with scripts is the UI area's to decide.

Final verdict: keep. A terminal a person types into runs with the operating-system user's permissions, outside the agent sandbox, with the scrubbed environment, asks no approval, survives a change of the agent's mode and writes no session event. Consequence kept in view: UI access is command execution, so the routes are owner only.

Final verdict: keep acquire-then-use and no stored process identity. Simplified: the host, not the browser, picks the candidate blank session of a workspace, takes its lease, re-checks it under the lease and creates a new session when another process holds it. Several processes share one home (DH-ADR-12), so the race is real in Go.

Final verdict: the goal stands (no base64, ranged reads, one authorisation path) and the mechanism goes. Bytes are an ordinary HTTP response with Range from a route that names the session, so it shares routing, access and errors with every other route; the multipart byte codec of the typed call is not needed.

Final verdict: the generated duplex stream is not the Go transport. Updates flow down on one event stream and input goes up as ordinary requests. Kept: an explicit per-request context with the caller's principal and a cancellation signal, and resume owned above the transport. The one duplex channel is the terminal socket, with acknowledgements in both directions; the SDK has its own protocol.

Final verdict differs from the first: not ported. The rule guards a slow per-session format migration that writes a new generation. The Go store has no such step: payloads are converted per event type on read and the layout migrates once, when the store is opened, after a backup. A rule with no subject is not carried; if a per-session migration is ever added, its area decides.

Final verdict differs from the first: the connect endpoint is not ported. It gives scripted callers their own peer on the browser API; in Go a program drives the harness through the SDK protocol or ACP on stdio and UI routes serve browsers only. The security rule is kept in another form: a caller that holds no event stream is never an answerer of approvals, and area A17 registers answerers per channel.

Final verdict: keep the model whole (a principal on every peer, no implicit fallback, resources declared per operation, one decision point, roles and bindings, a disposed peer always refused). Go declares resources in the route declaration and refuses to register a route without one, which turns upstream's review rule into a load error.

Final verdict differs from the first: nothing is redone for the new transport. The decision tunes compression of the multiplexed socket; that socket is gone, the event stream is never compressed (a compressor would delay small frames) and the terminal socket is uncompressed by default. Bandwidth over a tunnel is not addressed and is stated as a limit.

Final verdict: keep the separation of snapshot and observation for history, projections and state, and the rules that subscribing forces no read and no read wakes an agent. In Go the snapshots are area A06's query and projection reads, the observations are the store's Follow and projection.Changed, and the hub composes them for a page.

Final verdict: client registrations that follow access have no counterpart, because the host decides per request what to render. What must be designed instead is designed: an access change raises access.Changed and the hub re-sends baselines or ends streams, so an open page loses what was revoked.

Final verdict differs from the first: changed, not kept. Upstream dropped the session-membership check because proving it meant scanning history. Area A07 keeps a reference row per session and object, so the check is one indexed lookup, and an attachment is served only when the session in the URL references it. The store-wide read of any image by any authorised caller is therefore not carried.

Final verdict differs from the first: not adopted. The proposal shows the progress of a per-session migration, which the Go store does not have. Its useful rule, that progress of a host operation never enters the session log, holds anyway: such progress is a state region on the stream.

Final verdict: retained client objects and facets do not exist. Returning to a session is one page request: a range read of the tail by sequence number plus stored projections, with no agent woken. A host-side cache of rendered fragments is not designed until a budget test shows that this read is too slow.

Final verdict: the fix repairs a browser mirror that races the host's list. With one source the cause is gone, provided the host marks a session as not blank when a prompt is accepted (the first inbox insertion), before the turn starts; this is asked of area A06's list summary.

Final verdict: both halves lose their cause. The cache identity token works around proxy access to a service, and the waiting rule orders independent client requests. In Go one handler reads the page at one cut, and the completion routes are declared not to wake a session, so nothing competes for a cold read.

Final verdict: keep. A reused blank session runs the preset the request asks for, or the default, never the one its log recorded, and a candidate that fails a check is left unchanged; the checks run under the lease.

Final verdict: cooperative time slicing exists only because Node runs host work on one thread. Kept as ordinary Go behaviour, not as a mechanism: the list is cancelled through the request context and never returns a partial page.

Final verdict: keep host-owned processes with re-attachable views, create that is idempotent on an id, cleanup in the background with a retry, and listing that wakes no agent. Changed: the id is minted by the host when it renders the form, and close requests are host state, so nothing depends on browser storage.

Final verdict: keep the policy as written: reclaim only with no hold and after continuous, positively confirmed idleness; running or unknown activity restarts the clock; explicit close and owner disposal keep their authority. A hold is an open terminal socket, which replaces the separate retain stream.

Final verdict: keep watching only what is open, and watches that carry invalidation while content is read again through the bounded readers. In Go an open directory or preview is a stream interest; collapsing it releases the watch; a provider that cannot watch is polled.

Final verdict: keep. Continue is an empty user message with source retry through ordinary admission, allowed only after one of the six failure codes, when the agent is idle and nothing human is pending; the failed turn stays closed and no instruction text is invented.

Final verdict: confirmed. The note assigns history prefetch to client classes that do not exist when the host renders HTML. What a user sees is kept by the history route: turn-aligned older pages fetched on demand.

title: The gateway's machinery is dropped; its guarantees are restated as rules of the route and the stream
A route is a declared effect of the component that owns its feature
Resource ids live in the URL path, one writer draws each region, and every submit is idempotent
One hub, three recovery classes; the journal is pulled by cursor, state is replaced whole, a tab's interests select what it gets
Access: the owner is unrestricted, a non-owner needs a binding on every resource, and one argument-free function both renders and enforces
A browser on another machine is admitted as the owner through the same token exchange; everything else is refused
A person's terminal runs as the person, is owned by a session, and is the only WebSocket
File and attachment bytes are plain HTTP, addressed through a session, and bounded
Every UI route is a declared effect that leaves with its component
One way to answer: pages, fragments, forms and errors
Access is decided for every route and every stream, and only the owner path is open at first
A non-owner principal sees only what a policy grants, and a revocation reaches open pages
An open page shows every event once and in order, and stays live without blocking anything
A person can start, read, prompt, steer, cancel, continue and fork a conversation
A person can organise projects and pick a directory in the browser
A person can watch and stop background jobs, and edit settings and credentials
A person has terminals in the browser that survive a reload and are cleaned up
A person can browse, preview, search and download the files a session can read
An incomplete or duplicate route declaration fails registration, and a route leaves with its owner
Through the real loader, disabling a route component removes its routes and topics while others keep serving
Every registered route refuses a caller with no peer and a non-owner with no binding before its handler runs
A fragment has the same bytes in a page and alone, and actions answer by the kind table
Form bodies are decoded strictly and a bad field re-renders the form with its message
Each error code maps to its status, a Problem shows no internals, a failing view writes nothing
One request id submitted repeatedly, after a claim and after a restart, causes one inbox insertion
Access decisions follow roles and bindings, fail closed, and Allows equals Decide
A non-owner's list holds only admitted rows, and a list route must use the filter
An access change ends or re-baselines the affected open streams
Stream framing and the behaviour of the journal, state and notice classes
Cursor resume: replay, reset, and no duplicate or gap when events commit during catch-up
A change during a baseline read is not lost, and baselines are complete
A reader that stops is closed at the deadline, no producer blocks, memory per connection is bounded
A stream over the per-peer cap parks the longest-open session stream and never the attention stream
Tab interests: watch, cap eviction, reset for an unknown tab, expiry after the grace period
A stream handler ends with its owner, client or peer, and stream routes wait for ready
Conversation commands: blank reuse under the lease, requested preset, continuation eligibility, distinct fork titles
The opening page and the stream meet at one cut with no gap and no overlap
Activation: None creates no agent, LiveOnly refuses when idle, MayResume resumes once
Workspace routes: archive refusal with running work, order, and an owner-only directory picker
Job and settings routes: session-scoped roster, user kill, stale revision, no secret in any response
User terminals: caps, idempotent create, the reclamation clock, and the socket protocol and its lifetime
Workspace files: pages, ranges, scope, watch with polling fallback, and attachment membership
A browser shows every event once across a network cut, a parked tab and a host restart
A browser on another machine is admitted only by the stated path, and a same-site page cannot forge a request
web writes one content security policy and refuses every state-changing request that is not same-origin with a form token
A render failure is drawn as a placeholder, and reconnects are bounded on both sides
Every HTML answer carries the composed policy and fixed headers; only hashed import maps are allowed inline; a non-GET request without same origin and a valid form token is refused
A failing render draws a placeholder once, moves the cursor and keeps the stream open; a tab that reconnects too fast is refused with Retry-After
A person's terminal survives a reload and is cleaned up
A file preview follows changes made outside the harness
Disabling a feature removes its routes from a running product
